items.stem: Define the term “the Miller experiment”.
items.answer: The 1953 experiment in which electric discharge in a flask of CH₄, H₂, NH₃ and water vapour at 800 °C produced amino acids.

items.stem:
Isha reads two old ideas: one says maggots arise from rotting meat, another says life came to Earth on spores from space.
(i) Name these two ideas. (1 mark)
(ii) Who disproved the first, and how? (2 marks)
(iii) Which theory is now widely accepted? (1 mark)
items.answer: (i) Spontaneous generation; panspermia. (ii) Louis Pasteur: in pre-sterilised sealed flasks no life arose, while life arose in flasks open to air. (iii) The Oparin–Haldane theory of chemical evolution.

items.stem: Arrange the following in the correct sequence of events in the origin of life: chemical evolution, formation of macromolecules, formation of Earth, first cellular life. Give a reason.
items.answer: formation of Earth → chemical evolution → formation of macromolecules → first cellular life

items.answer: (i) Forelimbs of whale, bat and human. (ii) Wings of sparrow and butterfly. (iii) Homology – divergent evolution (same structure, different functions, common ancestry); analogy – convergent evolution (different structures evolving to perform the same function).

items.stem: How does industrial melanism in England support evolution by natural selection?
items.answer: Before industrialisation, white-winged moths were more common as they were camouflaged on lichen-covered trees. After industrialisation soot darkened tree trunks and killed lichens, so dark-winged moths escaped predators and increased. The environment selected the better-adapted form.

items.stem: State the Hardy–Weinberg principle. List the five factors that affect it.
items.answer: Allele frequencies in a population remain constant from generation to generation (p² + 2pq + q² = 1) if there is no disturbance. Factors: gene migration (gene flow), genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination, natural selection.

items.stem: Explain Darwin's theory of natural selection. How is the mutation theory of de Vries different from it?
items.answer: Darwin: organisms produce more offspring than can survive; there is variation, some of which is heritable; there is struggle for existence; individuals with useful variations survive and reproduce more (natural selection; fitness = reproductive fitness); over generations this leads to new species (branching descent). de Vries (evening primrose): evolution is caused by large, sudden mutations (saltation) that are random and directionless, not by small directional variations.
items.markingKey: 3 marks Darwin; 2 marks de Vries.

items.answer: Panspermia: spores came from outer space; favourite idea of some astronomers. Chemical evolution (Oparin–Haldane): first form of life came from non-living organic molecules; formation preceded by chemical evolution.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each correct, paired difference, e.g. panspermia – spores came from outer space; favourite idea of some astronomers; chemical evolution (Oparin–Haldane) – first form of life came from non-living organic molecules; formation preceded by chemical evolution.

items.stem: What is meant by “Australian marsupials”?
items.answer: Pouched mammals that evolved from an ancestral stock within Australia into many forms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: pouched mammals that evolved from an ancestral stock within Australia into many forms.

items.stem: Arrange the following in the correct sequence of human evolution: Homo sapiens, Homo erectus, Homo habilis. Give a reason.
items.answer: Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Homo sapiens
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the order Homo habilis → Homo erectus → Homo sapiens; 1 mark for the reason: Order of appearance in the fossil record.

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “Early Earth had a free-oxygen atmosphere.”
items.answer: Early atmosphere had water vapour, CH₄, CO₂ and NH₃; there was no free oxygen.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: Early atmosphere had water vapour, CH₄, CO₂ and NH₃; there was no free oxygen.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT an idea about the origin of life?
items.answer: mutation
items.markingKey: (a) Mutation is a factor that disturbs Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, not an idea about the origin of life.

items.stem: The following statement is incorrect. Rewrite it correctly and give a reason: “Analogous organs indicate common ancestry.”
items.answer: Homologous organs indicate common ancestry; analogous organs arise by convergent evolution.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the corrected statement, 1 mark for the reason: Homologous organs indicate common ancestry; analogous organs arise by convergent evolution.

items.stem:
A theory of the origin of life states: early reducing atmosphere; formation preceded by chemical evolution; supported by Miller's experiment.
(i) Which theory is it? (1 mark)
(ii) State one more feature you would expect to observe. (1 mark)
(iii) How would the observations differ if it were spontaneous generation? Give two points. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) Chemical evolution (Oparin–Haldane) (ii) first form of life came from non-living organic molecules (iii) no pre-existing life needed; life arose from decaying matter
items.markingKey: (i) chemical evolution (Oparin–Haldane) – 1 mark. (ii) any one of: first form of life came from non-living organic molecules – 1 mark. (iii) for spontaneous generation: life arose from decaying matter; disproved by Louis Pasteur; believed for a long time – 1 mark each for any two.

items.stem: Which of the following is a factor that disturbs Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium?
items.answer: gene migration (gene flow)
items.markingKey: (a) Gene migration (gene flow) is a factor that disturbs Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium; the others are not.

items.stem: Explain the term “gene flow”.
items.answer: The movement of alleles between populations by migration.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the movement of alleles between populations by migration.

items.stem: Give two differences between Homo erectus and Neanderthal man.
items.answer: Homo erectus: probably ate meat; about 1.5 million years ago. Neanderthal man: buried their dead; brain size 1400 cc.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each correct, paired difference, e.g. Homo erectus – probably ate meat; about 1.5 million years ago; Neanderthal man – buried their dead; brain size 1400 cc.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as pair of homologous organs or pair of analogous organs: forelimbs of whale and bat, flippers of penguin and dolphin, hearts of different vertebrates, thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita.
items.answer: forelimbs of whale and bat – pair of homologous organs; flippers of penguin and dolphin – pair of analogous organs; hearts of different vertebrates – pair of homologous organs; thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita – pair of homologous organs.
items.markingKey: ½ mark each: forelimbs of whale and bat – pair of homologous organs; flippers of penguin and dolphin – pair of analogous organs; hearts of different vertebrates – pair of homologous organs; thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita – pair of homologous organs.

items.stem:
(a) Distinguish between Homo sapiens and Australopithecines on any three points. (3 marks)
(b) A form in human evolution is described: about 2 million years ago. Identify the form – Homo sapiens or Australopithecines? Justify your answer. (2 marks)
items.answer: (a) Homo sapiens: between 75,000–10,000 years ago (ice age); arose in Africa, moved across continents; prehistoric cave art about 18,000 years ago. Australopithecines: about 2 million years ago; lived in East African grasslands; hunted with stone weapons and ate fruit. (b) Australopithecines.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each of three paired differences. (b) 1 mark: Australopithecines; 1 mark: “about 2 million years ago” is a feature of Australopithecines.

items.stem: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium the frequency of allele A is 0.7. What is the expected frequency of genotype AA?
Which of the following statements about evidences of evolution is correct?
items.answer: Analogy is a result of convergent evolution.
items.markingKey: (d) Analogy is a result of convergent evolution. The other statements are false. Homologous organs indicate common ancestry; analogous organs arise by convergent evolution. They are analogous; they perform the same function but differ in structure. Karl Ernst von Baer disapproved it, noting embryos never pass through adult stages of other animals.
options: Embryological support for evolution by Ernst Haeckel was fully accepted.
Wings of butterfly and bird are homologous.
Analogy is a result of convergent evolution.

items.stem: Which of the following shows the correct sequence of events in the origin of life?
items.answer: formation of Earth → chemical evolution → formation of macromolecules → first cellular life
items.markingKey: (b) formation of Earth → chemical evolution → formation of macromolecules → first cellular life. Inorganic → organic molecules → macromolecules → cells.
options: first cellular life → formation of macromolecules → formation of Earth → chemical evolution
formation of Earth → chemical evolution → formation of macromolecules → first cellular life
formation of macromolecules → formation of Earth → first cellular life → chemical evolution
formation of Earth → formation of macromolecules → first cellular life → chemical evolution

items.stem: Which term describes the movement of alleles between populations by migration?
items.answer: gene flow
items.markingKey: (a) Gene flow: the movement of alleles between populations by migration.

items.stem: Which ancestor in human evolution is described as: first human-like being; brain capacity 650–800 cc; probably did not eat meat?
items.answer: Homo habilis
items.markingKey: (b) Homo habilis (about 2 million years ago): first human-like being; brain capacity 650–800 cc; probably did not eat meat.

items.stem:
A pattern of natural selection is described: one extreme is favoured; more individuals acquire a value other than the mean; the peak shifts in one direction.
(i) Which type of selection is it? (1 mark)
(ii) State one more feature you would expect to observe. (1 mark)
(iii) How would the observations differ if it were stabilising selection? Give two points. (2 marks)
items.answer: (i) Directional selection (ii) seen in pesticide resistance (iii) peak gets higher and narrower; favours the average
items.markingKey: (i) directional selection – 1 mark. (ii) any one of: seen in pesticide resistance – 1 mark. (iii) for stabilising selection: more individuals acquire the mean character value; peak gets higher and narrower; extremes are eliminated – 1 mark each for any two.

items.stem: A theory of the origin of life states: early reducing atmosphere; first form of life came from non-living organic molecules. Which theory is it? Give a reason.
items.answer: Chemical evolution (Oparin–Haldane)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: chemical evolution (Oparin–Haldane); 1 mark: the features early reducing atmosphere; first form of life came from non-living organic molecules are characteristic of it.
